open-question.question: The mission's goal opens with a hands-on check of what Claude Desktop accepts from outside (a prompt, a folder, a model, an effort, a permission mode), and most of the feature's design hinges on what that check finds. Is the check run before the mission's remaining open questions are answered, with its findings written into the relevant starting state, or as the mission's first task after task derivation, with the decisions made beforehand written to hold for whichever outcome it finds?
open-question.alternative: The whole hands-on check (the `claude://code/new` link and the `claude --desktop` option, each tried for a prefilled or already-sent prompt, the folder the session opens on, and any model, effort, or permission mode it takes) is run now, by the person at the machine, outside any task, before the recommendation pass and the answer sweep run over the mission's questions; its findings are written into `## Relevant starting state` beside the static reading of Claude Desktop 5.11492.5 already there, and every open question is then recommended and answered against observed behaviour. If no prompt can be passed, the mission stops at that point, before any decision is recorded. Every decision that hinges on Desktop's behaviour (which opening mechanism, what happens to uncarried values, the over-long prompt, the stop conditions) is made against what Desktop was seen to do rather than against a guess, so no decision has to be written conditionally and the stop, if it comes, costs no decision work at all. The check is work outside the workflow's steps: no skill runs it, and since `specify-mission-starting-state` explores again only when `since` prints commits past its anchor, the findings reach the section by a hand edit or through a commit of the check's record that moves the ground (where that record lives is the sibling question on the check's record); the whole preparation waits until a person sits down with Claude Desktop, and picks formed before the findings land would need stripping.

The full hands-on check runs before answering, as in a pre-answer check with its findings written into `## Relevant starting state`, but only the questions whose answer hinges on its outcome wait for it; the questions that hold whatever it finds (how Desktop is selected for an action, the Harnesses row, the listing texts, the send feedback) are recommended and answered now, each through a single-question answer skill rather than the whole-mission sweep. Preparation keeps moving on the outcome-independent questions while the check waits for a person at the machine, and the decisions that do hinge on Desktop are still made against observed behaviour. Sorting the questions into dependent and independent is a judgment that can miss a dependency (a selection mechanism may yet hinge on whether Desktop takes a folder), the answer sweep cannot be used while some picks must be held, and a stop after the check leaves the independent decisions already recorded as wasted work.

Only the part of the check that decides whether the mission goes on and which mechanism can carry a prompt (does a prompt arrive through the link and through `claude --desktop`, prefilled or sent, and on which folder) is run now and written into `## Relevant starting state` before answering; the rest (whether `claude --desktop` takes a model, an effort, or a permission mode, how a long prompt behaves in practice) is the mission's first task after task derivation, with the decisions it touches written to hold for either outcome. The stop condition and the facts most decisions turn on are settled before any decision is made, at the cost of a short check, while the details whose outcome only shapes what the feature carries stay inside the task pipeline with a verified bar of their own. The line between the two parts is drawn before anyone has seen Desktop, so a fact left to the task may prove to decide a question already answered, and the decisions over the deferred part must still be written conditionally; the pre-answer part shares the hand-edit route into the starting state of a full pre-answer check.

The full hands-on check runs before answering, its findings written into `## Relevant starting state` and every question answered against them, and task derivation also places a first task that repeats the check against the Claude Desktop version installed when execution starts, stopping the run where the findings no longer hold. Decisions are made against observed behaviour, and the feature is still built against the behaviour that holds when it is built, which matters for an application updated as often as Claude Desktop (its static reading names a build number, 5.11492.5, not a stable interface). The check is run twice, the second time by a task that needs a person to watch Desktop (an unattended `complete-all-tasks` run cannot see whether a prompt arrived prefilled), and a changed finding at that point means revising recorded decisions after task derivation, which the workflow has no step for beyond revert and re-answer.

No check runs before answering: every open question is recommended and answered now against the static reading in `## Relevant starting state`, each decision that hinges on Desktop's behaviour written to hold for whichever outcome the check finds (a conditional pick of mechanism, values, and stop), and the hands-on check is the mission's first task after task derivation, its outcome choosing among the prepared branches and, where no prompt can be passed, stopping the mission there. The check runs inside the workflow, as a task with a derived and verified acceptance bar recorded in its `Task-completion:` commit, and preparation proceeds at once through the ordinary review, annotation, and answer sweep with no hand edit of the starting state. Conditional decisions are harder to write and to derive tasks from, every branch the check does not take is decision work spent for nothing, a stop after derivation leaves a task list holding feature tasks that must be removed before `finish-mission` will run, and the task needs a person to observe Desktop, so it cannot run in an unattended `complete-all-tasks` pass; how far the stop reaches depends on the sibling question on the check's stop conditions.

open-question.question: Where are the findings of the hands-on check of Claude Desktop recorded so that they outlive the mission's directory (the day, the Claude Desktop version checked, what was passed, and what arrived), both when the mission goes on and when it stops because no prompt can be passed?
open-question.alternative: No home outside the mission, in either outcome: the findings (the day, the Claude Desktop version checked, what was passed, and what arrived) are written into the mission's own requirements.md, in whichever section the check's timing puts them, and the Mission-finish: commit's summary body carries them as bullets, whether the mission finishes with the feature in place or stops after the check because no prompt can be passed. They outlive the directory as history only, read back through the missions tool's summary, record, and show at the finish commit and its parent. Adds no file, convention, or second copy: the finish commit already is the record of a finished mission, finish-mission writes it the same way in both outcomes, and the record and show queries already serve it to every later goal discussion and starting-state read. Nothing in the tree says what Desktop took or on which version, so someone editing the Desktop harness code, or re-checking after a Desktop update, finds the findings only by searching history, and the finish summary's bullets tend to compress them, the full detail standing only at the finish commit's parent; where the findings first land inside requirements.md depends on the Hands-on check timing question.

In the outcome where the mission goes on, the findings are kept as a dated comment block in the extension's source beside the Claude Desktop harness entry (in src/harnessCheck.ts, next to HARNESSES), naming the day, the Desktop version checked, what was passed, and what arrived, which a later re-check updates in place, mirroring the dated hands-on block each host's scripts/hosts/<host>/settings.toml carries in its header comment. In the outcome where the mission stops, no harness code is written, so the findings go into the mission's own record and its Mission-finish: summary body as under the mission-record option. Follows the repository's own convention for recording a hands-on check, and puts the findings exactly where a later editor of the Desktop code reads, with an established habit of updating the block when the application is checked again. Gives the two outcomes two different homes, so a stopped mission's findings are reachable from history only, which is where a later attempt at the same feature most needs them, and the extension has no such comment convention yet, so it is a new practice carried into TypeScript source rather than a reused one.

In both outcomes the findings are written to one tracked maintainer-facing document outside the mission directory and outside the VSIX (a note under ideas/, or a section of gurita-vscode/BUILDING.md), holding the day, the Desktop version checked, what was passed, and what arrived, and, when the mission stops, why it stopped; the Mission-finish: summary points at it rather than repeating it. One in-tree home whatever the outcome, so a stopped mission leaves a readable account standing exactly where a later attempt, or a re-check after a Desktop update, would start, without anyone having to know which finish commit to read. Creates a document no tool, skill, or reader is bound to, which ages silently as Claude Desktop updates, and fits neither candidate home cleanly: ideas/ holds design drafts that precede a mission and BUILDING.md documents the build.

In the outcome where the mission goes on, gurita-vscode/USAGE.md, the documentation the goal already brings up to date, states what Claude Desktop accepts from outside as observed by the check, stamped with the day and the Desktop version checked, together with what was passed and what arrived. In the outcome where the mission stops, USAGE.md gains nothing and the findings go into the mission's own record and its Mission-finish: summary body as under the mission-record option. The findings reach the people who use the feature, version-stamped, in a file the mission edits anyway, so a person can tell whether their own Desktop version is the one whose behaviour the documentation describes. Puts maintainer-facing test detail (what exactly was passed) into the installed extension's user reference, and like the dated-block option leaves the stopped outcome with no in-tree record; what USAGE.md says of values Desktop does not carry also touches the Uncarried line values question.

In both outcomes the findings are written into the project's CLAUDE.md, the context file every later session reads, as finish-mission's lasting-change edit riding in the Mission-finish: commit: the day, the Desktop version checked, what was passed, what arrived, and, when the mission stops, why Claude Desktop is not a harness. Every later session reads it unprompted, so a later proposal to add Desktop again meets the stopped mission's reason before any work starts, and the edit rides the finish step that already writes lasting changes, in both outcomes alike. Runs against the repository's practice of keeping tool versions and observed-behaviour facts out of the context file, which records rationale only and is already very long, and a version-stamped observation there goes stale at the next Desktop update with nothing prompting its revision.

open-question.question: The goal stops the mission when the hands-on check finds that no prompt can be passed to Claude Desktop. Which other findings, if any, stop it the same way: a session that cannot be opened on the project's folder, a Desktop session in which the Gurita plugin's `/gurita:` skills are not available, or none?
open-question.alternative: No finding beyond the goal's own stops the mission. A session that cannot be opened on the project's folder does not stop it, and the feature opens the Desktop session wherever Desktop puts it, leaving the person to move it to the project's folder. A Desktop session without the `/gurita:` skills does not stop it either, and the feature sends the prompt as the line carries it, leaving the person to make the plugin available in Desktop. The stop list stays exactly the goal's: no prompt can be passed. It keeps the goal as written and lets the mission ship whatever the check finds short of the one stated failure, so a partial result (the prompt arrives but the folder or the skills need a hand step) still gives the person Desktop's visual and sound artifacts, which is the reason the harness exists. The feature can ship as a button that opens a session where the skill invocation in its prompt does nothing, or one working on the wrong folder, so the action the person clicked is not the action that runs. What the person is told about that hand step falls to the questions on the Desktop Harnesses row, send feedback, and harness availability, and the feature is only as usable as those answers make it.

Two findings stop the mission: no prompt can be passed, or no session can be opened on the project's folder (neither the `claude://code/new` link's `folder` parameter nor the `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option puts the session there). A Desktop session without the `/gurita:` skills does not stop it, and the feature sends the prompt as the line carries it, leaving the person to make the plugin available in Desktop. Every Gurita action reads and writes a mission inside the project, so a session on another folder cannot do the work at all and is likely to write into the wrong tree, while missing skills are a one-time setup step the person can fix in Desktop and then rely on. It ships a feature whose prompts invoke skills Desktop may not have, so a fresh Desktop install sends a `/gurita:` prompt that resolves to nothing until the person installs the plugin there, with nothing in the extension's checks today able to tell (every Harnesses check assumes a CLI). Whether that gap is shown falls to the Desktop Harnesses row question.

Two findings stop the mission: no prompt can be passed, or the `/gurita:` skills are not available in the Desktop session opened (Desktop does not load the Gurita plugin copy Claude Code has, and offers no way to install it). A session that cannot be opened on the project's folder does not stop it, and the feature opens the session wherever Desktop puts it, leaving the person to pick the project's folder in Desktop. Every action the harness serves is a `/gurita:` skill invocation, so without the skills the prompt is plain text and the feature does nothing Gurita-specific, while a folder the person picks once in Desktop's own picker is a small hand step that leaves the action intact. It ships a feature that can open the session on a folder other than the project's, so until the person moves it the skill runs against the wrong tree or finds no mission, and a person who misses the step gets a session that writes outside the project. Whether the folder can be reached at all from a remote window is the harness availability question's, and this option leaves that case to it.

Three findings stop the mission the same way: no prompt can be passed, no session can be opened on the project's folder, or the `/gurita:` skills are not available in the Desktop session. The feature is built only when the check finds a session that opens on the project's folder, with the prompt prefilled, and with the skills it invokes available; otherwise the mission stops at the check and records why. The feature ships only when a click does what the action promises, the named skill running on the project's mission, so no button opens a session that silently cannot do its job and no hand step has to be documented or detected. It is the strictest bar and the likeliest to end the mission with nothing built, even where a hand step (picking the folder once, installing the plugin in Desktop once) would have made the feature work, which gives up the visual and sound artifacts the goal is after for a gap the person could close themselves.

No stop list beyond the goal's is fixed now. The check runs, and a finding that the session cannot be opened on the project's folder or that the `/gurita:` skills are not available is weighed when it is found, as a goal revision or a new open question, deciding then whether the mission stops, narrows, or goes on with a hand step. The decision is made against what Desktop actually does rather than against guesses, since nothing about how a folder or the plugin reaches a Desktop session has been observed, and a finding nobody foresaw (the session opening but reading another plugin copy, for instance) gets the same treatment as the two named ones. It leaves the mission's end condition open, so the decisions taken before the check cannot be written to hold for every outcome, and it works only where the check's findings reach a point at which a question can still be asked; whether they do is the hands-on check timing question's, and run as a task after derivation the check leaves no such point without stopping the task run.

open-question.question: Two ways of opening a Claude Desktop session from outside are known and neither has been tried: the `claude://code/new` link, which takes a prompt and a folder, and the `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option. Which does Gurita for VS Code use to send an action to Claude Desktop where the hands-on check finds that both pass a prompt?
open-question.alternative: The `claude://code/new` link only, the `claude` CLI not used: Gurita builds the link with the action's prompt, its placeholder values written into the text, as `q` and the project's root folder as `folder`, and hands it to `vscode.env.openExternal`, the extension's first call of that API. It depends on Claude Desktop alone, the scheme Claude.app registers and its own Finder service uses, with no CLI on the shell's path, and it starts no child process: VS Code's own API opens the link on the person's machine, including from a remote window. Placeholder values live only in the terminal's `GURITA_*` variables today, so a new function has to write them into the prompt text. The link cuts the prompt at 14,336 characters and names no model, effort, or permission mode, so the line's flags cannot travel with it. The only sign of failure is openExternal's boolean. In a remote window the folder is a remote path, so this option's reach depends on where the harness is offered, which the availability question decides.

The same `claude://code/new` link, with the prompt's values written in and the project's root as `folder`, passed to the operating system's opener (`open` on macOS, `xdg-open` on Linux) as an `execFile` child, the way the extension already runs its git and Python reads. The `claude` CLI is not used. The opener's exit status and stderr are a failure signal Gurita can read, for example no application handling the `claude` scheme, and the extension keeps its existing pattern of `execFile` children with no openExternal call. It has the link's costs: a new function to write values into the prompt, the 14,336-character cut, and no model, effort, or permission mode. The opener also runs on the extension host, which in a remote window is the remote machine, where no Claude.app runs, so where it works depends on the availability question. Each platform needs its own command.

The `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option only. The action's one interactive line runs as today, through the bundled runner in a terminal at the project root, with `--desktop` added to its `claude` command and no run tracked. The link is not used. The line's text stays whole. The shell expands the `GURITA_*` variables, so no function writes values into the prompt and no 14,336-character link cut applies. The line's `--model`, `--effort`, and bypass flag ride on the same command wherever the CLI forwards them, and the folder is the terminal's working directory. A VS Code terminal still opens, which the goal sets the Desktop session against, and the runner's run tracking has to be bypassed for this one kind of send. It needs `claude` on the session shell's path. Nobody has observed whether `--desktop` without `--continue` or `--resume` opens a new session with the prompt in place.

The `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option only, run by the extension itself as a background child of the session shell at the project root. The line's `claude` command gets `--desktop` added, and the `GURITA_*` values are set in the child's environment. No terminal opens and the link is not used. No terminal opens, yet the shell still expands the values and the line's own flags travel with it. The child's exit status and stderr give a failure signal, and there is no link length cut. It adds a new kind of child process. Nobody knows whether the CLI exits once it hands off to Desktop or stays running, and it needs `claude` on the session shell's path. In a remote window it runs on the remote host, so where it works depends on the availability question. Whether `--desktop` alone opens a new session with the prompt has not been observed.

Both mechanisms, chosen per send. When the harness check finds `claude` on the session shell's path, Gurita runs `--desktop` as a background child of the session shell at the project root. Otherwise it opens the `claude://code/new` link, with the values written into the prompt and the project's root as `folder`, through `vscode.env.openExternal`. Desktop is reachable for a person who has Claude.app but no CLI. Wherever the CLI is present, the send keeps the line's flags and avoids the link's prompt cut. Two code paths to build, test, and document, with different carried values and different failure signals. The same action can then open differently on two machines, for example with or without the line's model, and the person cannot tell which route was taken.

No mechanism is fixed now. The choice is left to the hands-on check under one stated rule: use whichever mechanism, when tried, also carries more of the project's folder, the model, the effort, and the permission mode, and leaves the prompt prefilled rather than already sent. On a tie, use the link. The choice rests on what Claude Desktop is seen to do rather than on a static reading of its bundle and the CLI's help text, which so far has observed nothing that either route delivers. The questions on feedback, over-long prompts, the Harnesses row, and remote availability are each shaped by the mechanism, so they stay unsettled or must be written to hold for either. How much that costs depends on when the check runs, which the timing question decides.

open-question.question: How does a person select Claude Desktop for an action in Gurita for VS Code, given that no action carries a harness setting of its own, that a line's harness is today the command the line opens with, and that the variants of one action can differ in whether they are a single interactive line?

alternative.id: Desktop line word, edited variants only

open-question.alternative: Claude Desktop is selected through the line, keeping the rule that a line's harness is the command it opens with. A Desktop line opens with a word of its own that names no CLI (a fourth key added to the three harness lists in `harnessCheck.ts`, `lineValues.ts`, and `SWITCHABLE` in `settingsWindow.ts`). The line editor's harness dropdown offers Claude Desktop only on the line of a variant that holds exactly one line, an interactive one. That test is new, since `Variant` records only `singleTask` and `looped`. A pick rewrites the line through `rewriteHarness` into a `custom N` variant in `~/.gurita/variants.json`. The person then selects that variant in the action button's existing dropdown, remembered in `workspaceState` as now. `shipped_recipes.md` ships no Desktop variant, and the action, the click, and the Settings window gain no other selection control. It reuses the whole existing path (dropdown pick, custom variant, variant selection), adds no new kind of setting, and keeps eligibility per variant. Desktop can only ever be picked on a one-interactive-line variant. Desktop's Enabled or Disabled state hides its variants through the existing disabled-harness filter, keyed by the line's first word. Nobody can use Desktop until they have opened the Settings window and made a custom variant for each action they want, seven variants across six actions. The new first word is no shell command, so every reader of a line's first word (`isHeadless`, `line_kind` in `runner.py`, `harnessChoices`) has to learn a word the runner must never execute. How the line keeps or drops its `--model` and `--effort` depends on the sibling question on uncarried line values.

alternative.id: Desktop line word, shipped and edited variants

open-question.alternative: As in the edited-only option, a Desktop line opens with a word of its own naming no CLI and is offered in the line editor's harness dropdown only on a variant of exactly one interactive line. In addition, `shipped_recipes.md` ships a Claude Desktop variant beside each existing one-interactive-line variant: both variants of `Execute tasks` and the one variant of each of `discuss-open-question`, `discuss-mission-goal`, `discuss-new-task`, `ask-in-mission-context`, and `capture-mission-principle-updates`. The person selects Desktop by picking such a variant, shipped or custom, in the action button's existing dropdown. Desktop is selectable straight away from every eligible action's dropdown with no editing, including the question card's discuss button, the case the goal names. When Desktop is disabled under Harnesses, the existing filter takes its shipped variants out of every list. The shipped recipe file grows by seven variants and the eligible actions' dropdowns double, while the variants carry nothing but the harness change. Their line text, and what they hold of model and effort, depends on the sibling questions on session opening and uncarried line values. Every reader of a line's first word must learn a word the runner must never execute.

Claude Desktop is selected through the line, but the line keeps opening with `claude`. An interactive `claude` line gains a trailing mark of its own (for example `# desktop` in place of `# interactive`, read the way `INTERACTIVE_MARK` is read today) that sends it to Desktop instead of a terminal. The line editor offers the mark, as a Claude Desktop entry or switch, only on a variant of exactly one interactive `claude` line, and stores the result as a `custom N` variant. The person then selects that variant in the action button's dropdown. Nothing is shipped, and no other selection control is added. The line stays a valid Claude Code interactive command, so the harness lists, `rewriteHarness`, the model and effort reads, and `runner.py`'s line kinds need no new command word. Where Desktop cannot be reached, the same variant can still fall back to a terminal run. It breaks the rule that a line's harness is its first word. Disabling Claude Code would hide Desktop variants, and Desktop's own Enabled state would need a filter rule of its own. Only `claude` lines can carry the mark, so an `agy` or `codex` variant must be switched to Claude Code first. Each action again needs a custom variant before Desktop can be used.

alternative.id: Desktop mark, shipped and edited variants

open-question.alternative: As in the mark option with edited variants only, a Desktop line is an interactive `claude` line carrying a trailing Desktop mark, offered in the line editor only on a variant of exactly one interactive `claude` line. In addition, `shipped_recipes.md` ships a marked variant beside each of the seven existing one-interactive-line variants, all of them `claude` lines today. The person selects Desktop by picking such a variant in the action button's dropdown. Desktop is available from every eligible action with no editing. The shipped lines stay valid `claude` commands, so no reader of a line's first word changes. It doubles the eligible actions' dropdowns with variants that are copies but for a mark. It still breaks the first-word harness rule, so the enabled-state filter needs a Desktop rule of its own, and disabling Claude Code hides the Desktop variants too. The marked lines' model and effort content depends on the sibling question on uncarried line values.

This rejects the premise that the harness lives only in the line. Each action gets a harness setting of its own: a Claude Desktop switch beside its button's variant dropdown, remembered per action in `workspaceState` beside the variant selection. The switch is shown, and applies, only while the selected variant is exactly one interactive line. Otherwise it is hidden, and the action runs its lines in the terminal as now. The lines, the line editor, and `shipped_recipes.md` stay unchanged, and at send time the extension reads the prompt from the variant's one line. One click on any eligible action selects Desktop, with no variant to create and no recipe change, and the choice is kept per action. The person's existing variants, with their model and effort choices, keep working whichever way they are sent. It adds a second place a harness is decided, beside the line's first word. The line then names one harness and the run goes to another, and the stored selection must be read together with the variant selection, a variant switch silently turning the Desktop choice off or back on. The six call sites in `pane.ts` and `finishedWindow.ts` each need the check and the remembered state.

This also rejects the line-only premise, but stores nothing. Each action button gains a separate control for a one-off send, an "Open in Claude Desktop" entry in its dropdown or a second button beside it. The control is shown only while the selected variant is exactly one interactive line, and is chosen afresh on every click. The ordinary click keeps running the variant in the terminal. The lines, the line editor, `shipped_recipes.md`, and `workspaceState` stay unchanged. The choice is made at the moment the person knows they need Desktop's artifacts, for one discussion and not the next, with no stored state that can go stale or disagree with the variant selection. A person who always wants Desktop for an action has to choose it on every click. Every eligible button on the mission page, the question card, the side-bar view's New mission row, and the finished mission's window gains a second control. The harness is again decided outside the line.

This rejects the per-action premise altogether. One setting, held with Claude Desktop's row under Harnesses in the Settings window and stored in `~/.gurita/variants.json`, sends every action whose selected variant is exactly one interactive line to Desktop. Every other action runs in the terminal as now. There is no per-action, per-variant, or per-click choice, and the lines, the line editor, and `shipped_recipes.md` stay unchanged. It is the smallest surface: one switch in one place, no new variant, no new button control, and no per-action state. It suits a person who works in Claude Desktop by habit. It is all or nothing. A person who wants Desktop only for the discussions that need visual or sound artifacts has to flip a global setting before and after. Sending Execute tasks to Desktop then follows from sending discuss-open-question there. The harness is decided away from both the line and the action.

open-question.question: In which windows does Gurita for VS Code offer the Claude Desktop harness: everywhere the extension runs, or only where Claude Desktop can reach the project's folder? The extension runs on macOS, on Linux, and in remote windows (Remote-WSL, SSH), where the project's folder is not a path an application on the person's own machine can open, and it stays inert on native Windows.
open-question.alternative: Claude Desktop is listed and selectable in every window where the extension is active: local macOS, local Linux, Remote-WSL, and SSH windows alike. There is no window rule. A send from any window opens the `claude://code/new` link (or whatever mechanism is chosen) with the project root as its folder, even when that path names a directory on another machine or inside WSL. No window logic, no platform test, and nothing extra to test. It also does not rule out a setup the mission cannot foresee, such as a person whose Desktop reaches the folder through its own `environment` parameter or a mounted share. In remote windows `vscode.env.remoteName` is set and the folder path belongs to the remote or WSL side, so the action is offered where it predictably opens Desktop on the wrong folder or on none. Because the send is fire-and-forget with no run tracked, the person learns this only in Desktop. How far that is softened depends on the send-feedback and Harnesses-row siblings.

Desktop is offered only when the extension host runs on macOS in a local window (`process.platform === 'darwin'` and no `vscode.env.remoteName`). In local Linux windows and in every remote window (Remote-WSL, SSH) it is not offered: it is never selectable for an action. This is decided by a fixed rule read from the window, with no probe of the application. It matches the one place Desktop is known to exist and be checked: `/Applications/Claude.app` registering the `claude` scheme on the machine where the hands-on check will run. So the feature is offered only where its behaviour has actually been observed. A local Linux window is excluded even where a Desktop build is installed and handles `claude://`. Any later reach beyond macOS means changing the rule. A macOS window without Claude Desktop installed still offers it, so a missing app shows up only on send.

Desktop is offered in every local window the extension runs in, macOS and Linux (no `vscode.env.remoteName`), and in no remote window, Remote-WSL and SSH alike. This is a fixed rule read from the window: an application on the person's machine can open the project's folder exactly when the extension host runs on that machine. The rule is exactly the question's criterion, folder reachability, and it is decidable from one value the extension already reads in `onNativeWindows`. It needs no platform list that would have to change if Desktop's platform support changes. On local Linux it offers a harness whose existence there neither the starting state nor the hands-on check (run on macOS) has confirmed. So a Linux user may get an option that opens nothing. As in every rule-based option, a local window without Desktop installed still offers it.

Desktop is offered in local macOS and Linux windows and also in Remote-WSL windows. In Remote-WSL the extension translates the project's Linux path into the Windows host's `\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\…` path for the folder it passes, and the link opens on the Windows side through VS Code's local UI. SSH windows never offer it. It reaches the Windows users whose only supported route into the extension is Remote-WSL, and Windows is a platform Claude Desktop is built for. The harness is then not effectively limited to Mac users. Nothing has checked whether Desktop's Code tab accepts a WSL network path as its folder or runs its tools and the Gurita plugin there correctly, and the hands-on check on this macOS machine cannot check it. It also adds path translation, distro detection, and their tests for a route the extension has never exercised. Its viability depends on the session-opening-mechanism sibling's choice handing the folder through the local side.

Instead of a fixed window rule, the extension probes from its own host whether Claude Desktop is installed and handles the `claude` scheme. On macOS that means finding the app bundle registered for the scheme; on Linux, a registered `x-scheme-handler/claude` handler. It offers Desktop only where the probe succeeds. In remote windows the probe runs on the remote side, finds no Desktop, and the harness is not offered, so reachability of the folder and presence of the app are settled by the same probe. The harness appears exactly where a send can work: a local window with Desktop installed. That holds on every platform, with no platform list and no guess about Linux, and a person without Desktop never sees a choice that opens nothing. It adds a per-platform probe of an application rather than a CLI, which nothing in the harness check does today, and a probe can misjudge an install it does not recognise. How the probe's outcome is shown depends on the Desktop-Harnesses-row sibling's answer about which checks that row makes.

open-question.question: What does Claude Desktop's row under Harnesses in the Settings window hold, given that the three existing rows each check a CLI (the command found in the shell, a Gurita plugin copy read through the CLI's plugin listing, that copy's version against the packaged one) and carry Install and Update controls: which of those checks does the row make for an application that is no CLI, and does it carry Install and Update controls?
open-question.alternative: The row names Claude Desktop and carries the Enabled or Disabled state with its one switching control, kept in the `harnesses` object of `~/.gurita/variants.json` like the other three, and nothing else: it makes none of the three checks (no presence check, no plugin check, no version check), draws no check outcome, carries no Install or Update control, and adds nothing to the side-bar view's plugin notice count. It needs no change to `harness_check.py` or `install_plugin.py` and claims nothing the extension cannot read: every existing check and control assumes a CLI, and this row asserts no state of an application the extension has never inspected. A person learns that Claude Desktop is missing, or that the Gurita skills are unavailable in its sessions, only when a send fails or the skill is not found in the opened session, so the row gives none of the readiness information the other three rows exist to give.

The row keeps the Enabled or Disabled state and its switch, and makes one check of its own in place of the CLI check: whether Claude Desktop is installed on the machine, read from the application bundle (`/Applications/Claude.app`, with its version taken from the bundle as information only) or from a registered handler of the `claude` URL scheme, never through a command in the shell. It makes no plugin check and no version check of a Gurita copy, carries no Install or Update control, and a failed presence check is drawn on the row only, not counted by the side-bar view's plugin notice, which counts plugin and version failures. It answers the one readiness question that is Desktop's own, whether there is an application to send to, with a cheap static read like the one the starting state made of the bundle, while staying silent about a plugin copy the extension has no interface to read. The Gurita skills' availability in a Desktop session goes unchecked, the failure the other rows exist to catch; and the check depends on axes siblings own, the opening mechanism (a `claude --desktop` send would rest on the `claude` CLI that Claude Code's row already checks) and the windows the harness is offered in (in a remote window the check script runs on the remote host, where no application of the person's machine is visible).

open-question.alternative: The row keeps the Enabled or Disabled state and its switch, makes the presence check of Claude Desktop (the application bundle or the `claude` URL scheme handler, never a shell command), and in place of a plugin and version check of its own shows the plugin and version outcome of Claude Code's row as the copy Desktop's Code tab sessions load, read once by the existing `claude` check and drawn on the Desktop row by reference to it. alternative.id: Presence plus Claude Code's plugin outcome and controls

open-question.alternative: The row keeps the Enabled or Disabled state and its switch, makes the presence check of Claude Desktop (the application bundle or the `claude` URL scheme handler, never a shell command), shows the plugin and version outcome of Claude Code's check as the copy Desktop sessions load, and carries Install and Update controls of its own that run `install_plugin.py` for the `claude` key in a terminal, the same run Claude Code's controls start, drawn on the Desktop row so the person fixes a failing outcome where it is shown; the side-bar view's plugin notice still counts the copy once. Every row under Harnesses keeps one shape, an outcome and the controls that act on it, so a person who looks only at the Desktop row can bring it to passing without knowing that it shares Claude Code's copy. Two rows then carry controls that change one and the same copy, so an install from the Desktop row also changes Claude Code's outcome, which the window must explain, and the whole row stands on the same unobserved premise that Desktop's sessions load the copy the `claude` CLI lists.

open-question.question: When an action is sent to Claude Desktop and Desktop takes no model, effort, or permission mode from outside, what becomes of the `--model`, `--effort`, and bypass-permission values the action's line carries: are they dropped without sign, or is the person shown, in the Settings window or on the action's button, that the Desktop session will not carry them?
open-question.alternative: The line keeps its `--model`, `--effort`, and bypass flag as written, and on a send to Claude Desktop whichever of them Desktop does not take (as the hands-on check finds) is dropped with no sign anywhere in the extension's windows or buttons; `gurita-vscode/USAGE.md` states once, where it documents the Desktop harness, that a Desktop session runs on Desktop's own model, effort, and permission mode and which line values it does not carry. Adds no UI, no state, and no test beyond the send itself, keeping the fire-and-forget feature as small as the goal frames it, and the values stay on the line unchanged for when the same variant is run in a terminal again. A person who picked a variant for its model or effort, or for its bypass flag, gets a session that silently differs: every shipped single-interactive-line variant carries `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--model`, and `--effort`, so an `Execute tasks` sent to Desktop runs `complete-all-tasks` under Desktop's permission prompts and its default model with nothing in VS Code saying so.

The line keeps its values; where the Settings window lets a person select Claude Desktop for an action's line, that line (or its variant) is marked with the values it carries that Desktop does not take, named as they stand on the line (for example the model, the effort, and the bypass flag), only those the hands-on check finds uncarried; the action's button and the send show nothing. Tells the person at the one moment a deliberate choice is made, with the exact values, and adds no clutter to the mission pages' buttons, which keep their current look. Reaches only someone who opens the Settings window: a Desktop selection made earlier, or a shipped variant used from a button, still sends without sign at the click; where the mark can sit depends on the selection mechanism a sibling question owns.

The line keeps its values; whenever an action's selected variant goes to Claude Desktop, its button in the page (its label, variant dropdown entry, or hover text) shows that the Desktop session will not carry the line's model, effort, or bypass values, naming those the hands-on check finds uncarried; the Settings window shows nothing of it. Tells the person right where and when they are about to send, every time, including for a selection made long before or remembered in `workspaceState`. Adds wording to buttons that today carry none of their lines' details, across the six button sites in `src/pane.ts` and `src/finishedWindow.ts`, and gives no sign at the moment the Desktop selection is made in Settings.

The line keeps its values; both the Settings window, where Desktop is selected for the line, and the action's button, while its selected variant goes to Desktop, show the values the line carries that Desktop does not take, naming those the hands-on check finds uncarried. Covers both the moment of choosing and the moment of sending, so no path to a Desktop send leaves the person unaware that the line's model, effort, or bypass flag will not apply. Two indicators to build, keep consistent, and test for one fact, the largest UI cost of the told options; the Settings half depends on the selection mechanism a sibling question owns.

The line keeps its values and neither the Settings window nor the button shows anything; when a click sends the action to Claude Desktop, a notice in VS Code names the line's values the Desktop session will not carry, only those the hands-on check finds uncarried. Tells the person once per send, at the exact moment the values are dropped, with no lasting change to any window's or button's layout. The person learns of it only after the session is already opening, too late to choose a terminal variant instead, and it repeats on every send; it rides beside whatever the person sees after the click, which the Desktop send feedback sibling question owns.

The premise that the line goes on carrying values Desktop does not take is rejected: when a line is set to go to Claude Desktop, the stored line is rewritten without whichever of `--model`, `--effort`, and the bypass flag Desktop does not take, so nothing is uncarried and no indicator is needed; what the line text shows is what the session gets. The line is truthful by construction, so the Settings window's line editor already shows exactly what the Desktop session carries, with no separate indicator to build or keep in step. Switching the line back to a terminal harness loses the values the person had set, and the rewrite applies only if Desktop is selected by rewriting a line, which the Desktop selection mechanism sibling question owns; a shipped variant sent to Desktop without a rewrite would still drop its values without sign.

open-question.question: What does Gurita for VS Code do when an action's prompt, with the values the person typed written into it (a goal, an issue description, a question), is longer than Claude Desktop accepts from outside, the `claude://code/new` link cutting its prompt at 14,336 characters?
open-question.alternative: No length check in the extension, now or later in this mission: the prompt, with the typed values written in, is sent to Claude Desktop whatever its length, and Desktop's own handler cuts it at its limit (14,336 characters for the `claude://code/new` link). Nothing is shown about the length, and USAGE.md at most states the limit. No code, no test, and no message for a case the shipped actions hardly reach: each single-interactive-line action's prompt is a short skill invocation (`/gurita:discuss-mission-goal`, `discuss-new-task`, `ask-in-mission-context`, `discuss-open-question`, and the rest) followed by one typed value, so only a value of some two thousand words or more, such as an issue description with a pasted log, comes near the limit. When the limit is passed the cut is silent and falls in the typed value, which stands last in every shipped prompt, so the Desktop session starts on a goal, issue description, or question missing its tail without the person or the model knowing; and the limit depends on the mechanism chosen under the session-opening sibling, so the documented figure may not be the one that applies.

Before sending, the extension builds the prompt with the typed values written in, measures it as Desktop measures it, and when it passes the limit sends nothing, telling the person the prompt's length and the limit so they can shorten the value or pick a terminal variant of the action themselves. No prompt ever reaches Desktop cut, and the rule is one comparison against one constant at the one place the Desktop send is made, easy to pin in a unit test. The value the person typed is lost with the refused click unless it is kept for the next try, the input panel resolving and closing on Run, so a long description has to be typed or pasted again; and the limit's figure rests on the session-opening mechanism a sibling question chooses.

The same check before sending, and on a prompt past the limit nothing is sent to Desktop; the message offers, beside cancelling, to run the same action in a VS Code terminal as an ordinary tracked run of its interactive `claude` line, with the value already typed, where no such limit applies. The person's typed value is never lost and the action still runs in one more click, while nothing is cut and nothing switches harness without their say. The terminal session gives up exactly the visual and sound artifacts Desktop was selected for, and the offer needs a terminal line for the action, which an action whose selected variant was rewritten for Desktop must still yield, a dependency on how the Desktop-selection sibling settles.

The same check before sending, and on a prompt past the limit the extension runs the action in a VS Code terminal instead, without asking, as an ordinary tracked run with the value typed, telling the person in one notice that the prompt was too long for Claude Desktop. The click always runs the action with the whole value and costs the person no extra decision. The person who chose Desktop silently loses its artifacts on the one action they gave the most text to, and one click then sometimes starts a tracked terminal run and sometimes an untracked Desktop send, so the page's disabled buttons and refusal of a second click behave differently by input length.

The same check before sending, and on a prompt past the limit the prompt is still sent, cut at the limit by Desktop or by the extension at the same point, and the person is told that the session received only the first part of what was typed, the rest left out. Desktop is always opened as selected, so a person who mostly needs the session and its artifacts can paste the rest into it by hand, and the cut is no longer silent. The model may already be acting on the cut prompt before the person reads the warning, if Desktop sends a prefilled prompt rather than leaving it to be sent, which the hands-on check has not yet observed; and the session then rests on a partial goal or description.

Where an action's selected variant goes to Desktop, the input panel shows the room left for the value (the limit less the rest of the prompt) and refuses Run past it on the page, keeping the text, and the same check before sending refuses any prompt still past the limit through a value typed outside the panel, such as a question or a discussion note asked in an input box. The person learns of the limit while typing, with the text still in front of them to shorten, so no value is lost and no click is refused after the fact. The input panel, today harness-blind, comes to know the action's harness and the rest of its prompt, and the send-time check is still needed beside it, so two places carry the rule and its tests; the figure rests on the session-opening sibling's mechanism.

The same check before sending, and on a prompt past the limit the extension puts the whole prompt on the clipboard and opens the Desktop session on the project's folder with no prompt, telling the person to paste it there; a prompt within the limit is sent prefilled as usual. The whole value reaches the Desktop session with its artifacts, with no length cap at all and no file written. It adds a manual paste the ordinary send does not need and overwrites whatever the person had on the clipboard, and it rests on Desktop opening a session on a folder alone, which the Finder service form suggests but the hands-on check has not observed.

The same check before sending, and on a prompt past the limit the extension writes the typed value to a file in the system temp location and sends a prompt in which the value is replaced by a sentence naming that file for the session to read; a prompt within the limit is sent as usual. The session opens in Desktop on the project's folder with the whole value reachable and no step for the person, whatever the value's length. The skill receives a pointer where it expects the literal goal, issue description, or question, so its handling rests on the model reading the file before it parses its text, which no skill states; and the Desktop session may need permission to read a file outside the project's folder, while a file inside it would dirty the tree.

open-question.question: Sending an action to Claude Desktop is fire-and-forget, with no run tracked. What does the person see in VS Code after the click: anything at all on a send that went out, and what on a send that failed, such as Claude Desktop not being installed or the link not being handled?
open-question.alternative: Success: VS Code shows nothing; Claude Desktop coming to the front with its new session is the only sign. Failure detection: none; the extension does not inspect the outcome of the hand-off to the operating system or check for Claude Desktop beforehand. Failure presentation: none; a send that went nowhere is noticed only by Desktop not appearing. The smallest change and the most literal reading of fire-and-forget: no message text, no check, and no new notification code path to test, and the button behaves like the existing ones, which report a started run by the terminal appearing rather than by a message. A failed send is indistinguishable from a slow one: a person without Claude Desktop installed, or whose `claude` scheme no handler takes, clicks and sees nothing happen with no reason given, while every other failure in the extension (a read, a commit, a variant edit) is reported by an error message.

Success: VS Code shows nothing; Desktop coming to the front is the sign. Failure detection: from the outcome of the send call itself only (the opener's returned result or the exit status of the command that opens the session), with no check made beforehand. Failure presentation: one error message (`showErrorMessage`, as the extension's other failures use) saying the action could not be sent to Claude Desktop, carrying the cause the call reported. Reports exactly the failures the extension can actually see, at no cost on the success path, and follows the extension's established convention of a silent success and an error message for a failure. Catches only what the hand-off reports: once the operating system has passed the link to a handler, a session that never opens, or a prompt Desktop drops, reads as a success; and how much the call reports at all depends on the sending mechanism the Session opening mechanism question picks (an opened link's yes-or-no result versus a CLI's exit status and message).

Success: VS Code shows nothing; Desktop coming to the front is the sign. Failure detection: before sending, the extension checks that Claude Desktop is present on this machine (its application bundle found, or the `claude` URL scheme registered to it), and after sending it also reads the outcome of the send call. Failure presentation: one error message naming which failed, Claude Desktop not found (nothing sent) or the send not taken, with the cause. Turns the commonest failure, Desktop not installed, into a specific message before anything is attempted, rather than relying on whatever generic result the operating system gives for an unhandled link. Adds a platform-specific presence check (an application path or scheme lookup) at send time that the extension does not make today and that a remote window cannot make on the person's own machine; its overlap with what the Settings window's Desktop row checks depends on the Desktop Harnesses row question, and where it is offered on the Desktop harness availability question.

Success: VS Code shows nothing; Desktop coming to the front is the sign. Failure detection: from the outcome of the send call, with no check beforehand. Failure presentation: an error message carrying the cause plus action buttons that keep the person going: one copying the action's prompt, its typed values written in, to the clipboard for pasting into a Desktop session opened by hand, and one running the action in a VS Code terminal instead, as an ordinary tracked run of its interactive line. A failed send does not lose the typed goal, issue description, or question: the person can finish the action another way in one click instead of retyping it or reselecting a harness. Two more code paths on the failure branch, and the terminal offer is only as simple as the way a line selected for Desktop maps back to its terminal form, which depends on the Desktop selection mechanism question; the clipboard copy also puts the prompt's values where other applications can read them.

Success: a short-lived confirmation that the action was sent to Claude Desktop, shown as a status-bar message that fades after a few seconds or an information message, with no run tracked and no button disabled. Failure detection: from the outcome of the send call, with no check beforehand. Failure presentation: one error message carrying the cause. Gives the person an explicit acknowledgement in VS Code itself, useful when Desktop opens behind the editor or on another display, or takes a moment to start, so the click is never followed by apparent silence. The confirmation says only that the hand-off went out, not that a session opened with the prompt, so it can affirm a send that Desktop then drops; it is also the one success message among the extension's actions, which report nothing on a started run.

Success: a short-lived confirmation that the action was sent (a fading status-bar message or an information message). Failure detection: a presence check of Claude Desktop before sending plus the outcome of the send call after it. Failure presentation: an error message naming which failed, with the cause, plus buttons copying the prompt with its values written in to the clipboard and running the action in a VS Code terminal instead. The fullest feedback the extension can give without tracking a run: every outcome it can observe is reported in VS Code, the commonest failure is named specifically, and a failed send can be finished another way at once. The largest amount of new code and tests for a fire-and-forget path, combining every cost above: a platform-specific presence check (overlapping the Desktop Harnesses row question and unavailable in remote windows), a success message the other actions do not show, and a terminal fallback whose simplicity depends on the Desktop selection mechanism question.

Success and failure are both drawn on the page holding the action's button (a mission page, or the finished-mission window for Capture principles), beside that button, in the page's existing bordered notice style: a line saying the action was sent to Claude Desktop, or one saying it could not be sent with the cause, standing until the page is next drawn or the next action is fired. Failure detection: from the outcome of the send call, with no check beforehand. No VS Code notification is shown, and no button is disabled. The feedback stays where the person clicked and remains visible after they return from Desktop, so it is never missed the way a fading message can be, and it reuses the notice styling the mission page already draws for conditions that would stop a run. Needs per-window state the pages do not hold for anything but tracked runs, posted into each of the button's hosts (mission pages, the side-bar view's New mission row, the finished-mission window), so it touches more of the webview code than a notification would; and like every reactive option it can show sent for a link Desktop then drops.
